chapter_summary:
Once you've established a baseline understanding of your Junos device's operational status and logging mechanisms, the next step in effective network management is to actively test connectivity and diagnose issues using built-in network utilities. Junos OS provides a suite of familiar tools like `ping`, `traceroute`, `telnet`, `ssh`, and its own powerful `monitor traffic` command, which are indispensable for real-time troubleshooting.

The `ping` command is arguably the most fundamental network troubleshooting tool. It sends ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo request packets to a target host and listens for ICMP echo replies. A successful `ping` confirms basic IP connectivity between your Juniper device and the target. When a `ping` fails, it could indicate a variety of issues: no route to the host, a firewall blocking ICMP, the host being down, or a physical layer problem. For example, if you can't `ping` a directly connected neighbor, it's highly likely there's a problem with the interface configuration or the physical link itself. Junos OS offers various `ping` options, such as `ping <ip-address> count <number>` to send a specific number of packets, or `ping <ip-address> routing-instance <instance-name>` if you're working with virtual routing instances. A common mistake is to only `ping` once; always send multiple `pings` to check for packet loss or intermittent connectivity.

While `ping` confirms reachability, `traceroute` helps you understand the path packets take to reach a destination. It works by sending packets with incrementally increasing Time-To-Live (TTL) values. Each router along the path decrements the TTL and, when it reaches zero, sends an ICMP "Time Exceeded" message back to the source. By analyzing these messages, `traceroute` reveals the IP addresses of the routers (hops) along the path. This is incredibly useful for identifying where connectivity breaks down or if traffic is taking an unexpected path. For example, if `ping` fails, `traceroute` can pinpoint the exact hop where packets stop forwarding. If you see an asterisk (`*`) for a hop, it means no response was received, possibly due to a firewall blocking ICMP or a congested link. The Junos `traceroute` command also supports options like `source <ip-address>` to specify the source IP for the trace, which is useful when testing from a specific interface.

For remote access and testing specific services, `telnet` and `ssh` are crucial. `SSH` (Secure Shell) is the preferred method for secure remote management of Junos devices, providing encrypted communication. `Telnet`, on the other hand, transmits data in plaintext and should only be used in controlled lab environments or for quick, non-sensitive service checks. You can use `telnet <ip-address> <port>` from the Junos CLI to test if a specific TCP port is open on a remote host. For instance, `telnet 192.168.1.100 80` will attempt to connect to port 80 (HTTP) on the remote server, confirming if the web server is listening and reachable on that port. If the connection is refused or times out, it could indicate a firewall blocking the port, the service not running, or a routing issue.

When you need to go deeper and analyze the actual packets traversing an interface, Junos OS provides the `monitor traffic` command (similar to `tcpdump` on Linux). This powerful tool allows you to capture and display packet headers and even full packet contents in real-time. You can filter traffic based on source/destination IP, port numbers, protocols, and more. For example, `monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 detail` will show detailed packet information on interface `ge-0/0/0.0`. To capture only HTTP traffic, you might use `monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 matching "port 80"`. This is invaluable for diagnosing complex application-layer issues, verifying firewall rules, or confirming that expected traffic is actually flowing. A common pitfall is to run `monitor traffic` without any filters, which can quickly overwhelm the console with irrelevant data and potentially impact device performance on busy interfaces. Always apply specific filters to focus on the traffic you need to analyze.

screens.title: Network Utilities and Troubleshooting Tools
screens.subtitle: Using ping, traceroute, telnet/ssh, and monitor traffic to find and fix connectivity problems

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on the practical tools Junos supplies for diagnosing network problems. You will learn how to confirm reachability with ping, inspect the path to a destination with traceroute, test service ports with telnet and secure management with SSH, and capture live packets using monitor traffic. These utilities are the core of everyday troubleshooting because they let you verify hypotheses quickly — for example, whether a host is reachable at all, which hop in the network is dropping traffic, or whether a specific service port is listening. I will also highlight common mistakes, like pinging only once or running packet capture without filters, and show you a simple workflow combining these tools to isolate faults. By the end of this chapter you will be able to select the right tool for each stage of an investigation, interpret typical outputs such as packet loss or star markers in a trace, and avoid actions that create noise or overload devices. Think about a time you could not reach a server: what would you test first, and how would these utilities help you form a fast, evidence-based next step?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use the right built-in utility to gather targeted evidence: ping for reachability, traceroute for path, telnet/ssh for service checks and access, and monitor traffic for packet-level confirmation.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Network Utilities
Network Utilities and Troubleshooting Tools
Practical commands for reachability, path analysis, service tests, and packet captures on Junos OS.
In this lesson

You will learn how to interpret ping and traceroute outputs, when to use telnet or SSH for testing services, and how to capture relevant traffic with monitor traffic while avoiding common pitfalls.

Why it matters

Fast, targeted troubleshooting avoids long outages. These utilities give you actionable evidence to locate failures and confirm fixes without guessing.

Explore Key Topics
Ping & traceroute, telnet/ssh for service tests, and monitor traffic for packet analysis.
Ping & Traceroute
Confirm reachability and reveal the packet path so you can locate the hop that fails.
Telnet & SSH
Test service ports quickly with telnet; use SSH for secure remote management.
Monitor Traffic
Capture packet headers and payloads with filters to verify application-level behavior.
Quick workflow
Baseline → reachability → path → service → packet capture
Use these steps iteratively: a failed ping calls for a traceroute; a path break calls for a service test; a port or application issue calls for monitor traffic with filters.
Coming up

screens.title: ping — Confirming basic IP reachability
screens.subtitle: How ping uses ICMP to test connectivity and what successful or failed responses imply

narration.text: Ping is the most direct way to check whether an IP host is reachable from your Junos device. It sends ICMP echo request packets and expects ICMP echo replies; receiving replies confirms that IP connectivity exists between source and destination and gives you round-trip time measurements. For example, running ping to eight dot eight dot eight dot eight five times gives you a small sample of latency and packet loss. A common misconception is to run a single ping and assume the network is healthy; intermittent loss often appears only across multiple probes. When ping fails, the cause could be an absent route, a down interface, a firewall blocking ICMP, or a host that is offline. If you cannot ping a directly connected neighbor, begin by checking the local interface configuration and link status — that narrows the problem to the physical or link layer. In practice, always send several pings, note packet loss and variation in round-trip times, and then use traceroute if you need to find the hop where packets stop. As a takeaway, treat ping as a fast, low-cost hypothesis test: it tells you whether to keep investigating upstream or focus on the local link.

keyIdea.title: Ping summary
keyIdea.text: Ping validates basic IP reachability and measures round-trip time; run multiple probes to reveal packet loss or intermittent issues.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ping — Reachability
Definition & behavior
Ping sends ICMP echo requests and awaits echo replies. Success shows reachability and round-trip time; failure narrows possible causes to routing, firewall, host, or link problems.
Common uses
  • Confirm that an IP address responds at the network layer.
  • Measure baseline latency and detect packet loss.
  • Quickly check neighbor interfaces and forwarding.
Common mistakes
Pinging only once and assuming success; ignoring packet loss percentages that indicate intermittent issues.
Key Takeaway

Use multiple pings to measure stability; a failed ping requires tracing the path or checking local interfaces and routes.

Example commands and output
# ping 8.8.8.8 count 5
PING 8.8.8.8 (8.8.8.8): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=0 ttl=118 time=15.232 ms
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=118 time=15.345 ms
--- 8.8.8.8 ping statistics ---
5 packets transmitted, 5 packets received, 0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 15.232/15.301/15.345/0.045 ms
Scenario card: If a directly connected neighbor does not respond to ping, immediate next checks are the interface operational state and configuration. That isolates physical or link-layer faults quickly.

screens.title: Using ping effectively — options and interpretation
screens.subtitle: Practical options like count and routing-instance and how to interpret loss and RTT variance

narration.text: Ping is simple, but using it effectively requires attention to options and interpretation. Junos allows you to set a count to send multiple probes, and to specify a routing instance when you want to test reachability from a virtual routing context. For example, ping the target five times to observe packet loss over multiple samples. Interpreting results means looking for loss percentage and round-trip time variance: steady low RTT with zero loss is healthy; intermittent dropped responses or widely varying RTTs point to congestion or instability. A common mistake is using ping alone to conclude that an application is unreachable; ICMP may be allowed while a TCP port is closed, or ICMP may be blocked while TCP service is functional. Therefore, follow a failed or inconclusive ping with traceroute to find where packets stop, then a targeted telnet to test the specific service port. Also avoid misinterpreting small packet loss on busy networks; check multiple times and correlate with interface statistics. Always document your ping samples so you can compare before and after configuration changes. Using ping effectively — options and interpretation means send multiple probes, use routing-instance when needed, and interpret loss and rtt variance before moving to path or service tests.. In practical terms, practical options like count and routing-instance and how to interpret loss and rtt variance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ping best practices
keyIdea.text: Send multiple probes, use routing-instance when needed, and interpret loss and RTT variance before moving to path or service tests.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ping — Options & Interpretation
Useful ping options
  • count <number> — send multiple echo requests to measure loss.
  • routing-instance <name> — test reachability from a specific virtual routing instance.
How to interpret
  • 0% packet loss and stable RTTs typically indicate healthy connectivity.
  • Intermittent packet loss suggests congestion, flaky links, or device problems.
  • Complete lack of replies suggests route absence, a host down, or ICMP filtering.
Misconception: ICMP reachability equals application availability — not always. Use port tests for application-level checks.
Concrete example
# ping 8.8.8.8 count 5
# ping 10.0.0.1 routing-instance mgmt count 5
Example scenario: if the first command shows 20% packet loss while the routing-instance test shows 0% loss, traffic may be following different paths or firewall rules applied per routing-instance.
Key Takeaway

Use ping options to sample and scope tests; compare multiple runs and contexts before concluding a fault.

screens.title: traceroute — Discovering the path with TTL
screens.subtitle: How traceroute incrementally reveals hops by leveraging Time-To-Live behavior

narration.text: Traceroute reveals the sequence of routers packets traverse by exploiting the Time-To-Live field. It sends packets with increasing TTL values; each intermediate router decrements TTL and returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message when TTL reaches zero, allowing you to see the router's IP address and timing. This method helps you locate precisely where forwarding stops: if traceroute shows replies up to hop three and then stars appear for hop four onwards, that indicates the problem is at or after the fourth hop. An asterisk means no response — often due to ICMP being blocked at that node or a congested link. A common misconception is that traceroute always lists every device on the physical path; some devices do not respond to TTL-expired messages or are configured to hide themselves. Junos traceroute supports options like specifying a source IP so you can trace from a particular interface; this is useful when multi-homed devices route differently. Use traceroute after a failed or flaky ping to translate a reachability failure into an actionable hop-level hypothesis. traceroute — Discovering the path with TTL means traceroute maps hops using ttl expirations; asterisks mean no replies and indicate where to focus your investigation.. In practical terms, how traceroute incrementally reveals hops by leveraging time-to-live behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Traceroute summary
keyIdea.text: Traceroute maps hops using TTL expirations; asterisks mean no replies and indicate where to focus your investigation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › traceroute — Path discovery
How traceroute works
Traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL. Each router that decrements TTL to zero replies with a TTL-exceeded message, showing the hop address and timing.
Interpreting hops
  • Complete hop lines show responding routers and RTTs.
  • An asterisk (*) indicates no response — possibly ICMP filtered or overloaded.
  • Stopping at a hop suggests the next device may be down or blocking traffic.
Misconception: traceroute shows every physical device; in reality, some nodes intentionally do not respond to TTL-exceeded messages.
Example output
# traceroute 8.8.8.8
traceroute to 8.8.8.8 (8.8.8.8), 30 hops max
 1  192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1)  0.643 ms  0.428 ms  0.395 ms
 2  10.0.0.1 (10.0.0.1)  1.234 ms  1.189 ms  1.156 ms
 3  * * *
Scenario card: If the trace stops at hop three with asterisks afterwards, investigate hop three's configuration and forwarding behavior. Check for firewall rules or routing issues on that device.
Key Takeaway

Use traceroute to convert a reachability symptom into a hop-level hypothesis. Asterisks point to non-responding hops that deserve targeted investigation.

screens.title: telnet vs SSH — When to test with telnet and when to connect with SSH
screens.subtitle: Understand the difference between insecure service testing and secure remote management

narration.text: Telnet and SSH serve different troubleshooting needs. Telnet connects to a specific TCP port in plaintext, making it a quick way to verify whether a service is listening and reachable. For example, using telnet to target port eighty lets you check whether a web server accepts TCP connections on that port. SSH provides encrypted remote management and is the recommended method to administer Junos devices. A common mistake is to use telnet in production for management or credential entry; because telnet transmits data in cleartext, it should be confined to isolated lab scenarios or simple port checks where security is not a concern. When telnet times out or is refused, the cause could be a firewall blocking the port, the service not running, or a routing issue. If telnet succeeds but the application fails at higher layers, capture packets with monitor traffic to inspect payload and protocol behavior. Use telnet for targeted checks and SSH for any interactive operational tasks that require privacy and integrity. telnet vs SSH — When to test with telnet and when to connect with SSH means telnet is useful for quick port checks but insecure; ssh is for secure management and should be used for operational access.. In practical terms, understand the difference between insecure service testing and secure remote management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Telnet vs SSH
keyIdea.text: Telnet is useful for quick port checks but insecure; SSH is for secure management and should be used for operational access.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › telnet vs SSH
Telnet (insecure)
Use telnet to test whether a TCP port is open. It makes a plain TCP connection and is not encrypted.
When to use
  • Quick service checks in labs or controlled networks.
  • Verify whether a server is listening on a specific port.
Warning: Do not use telnet for remote management in production because credentials and session data are sent in plaintext.
Example: telnet 192.168.1.100 80 attempts a TCP connection to port 80 to check an HTTP listener. A successful connection indicates the port is reachable; refusal or timeout indicates a firewall, closed service, or routing issue.
SSH (secure)
SSH provides encrypted access for operational tasks and should be used for any interactive device management or sensitive commands.
When to use
  • Secure remote administration of Junos devices.
  • When you need confidentiality and integrity for commands and credentials.
If a port test with telnet succeeds but SSH fails, check SSH service configuration, access lists, and host keys; if telnet fails while SSH succeeds, that reveals different firewall or service-level rules affecting specific ports.
Key Takeaway

Use telnet for isolated port checks only. Use SSH for secure operational access and sensitive tasks.

screens.title: Using telnet to test services — Example walk-through
screens.subtitle: A terminal-style check of a TCP service and how to interpret outcomes

narration.text: Telnet is useful when you need to confirm whether a remote host is listening on a particular TCP port. The command structure is simple: telnet followed by the IP address and port. In a lab, try telnet to a web server port to validate reachability and service presence. When you see a connection and a prompt such as indication of an open socket, the service is accepting TCP connections. If you see a connection refused message, the host is reachable but the port is closed or the service is stopped. If the command times out, the packet may be dropped by a firewall or a routing problem exists. A common misconception is assuming a successful telnet guarantees the application will operate correctly under normal load; telnet only confirms the socket is reachable. If telnet fails, use ping and traceroute to rule out path issues. If telnet succeeds yet the application misbehaves, capture packets with monitor traffic to inspect protocol exchanges. This stepwise approach limits guessing and produces clear next steps. Using telnet to test services — Example walk-through means telnet checks a tcp port: success means the socket is open; refusal or timeout points to service closure, firewall, or routing issues.. In practical terms, a terminal-style check of a tcp service and how to interpret outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Telnet walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Telnet checks a TCP port: success means the socket is open; refusal or timeout points to service closure, firewall, or routing issues.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › telnet — Service test
Terminal example
# telnet 192.168.1.100 80
Trying 192.168.1.100...
Connected to 192.168.1.100.
Escape character is '^]'.
<type quit and Enter to close>
# OR
# telnet 192.168.1.100 22
Trying 192.168.1.100...
Connection refused
Interpretation: Connected means the TCP socket accepted the connection; refused means the host replied but the service port is closed; timeout indicates possible firewall or routing drop.
Concrete scenario
If telnet to port eighty connects but web pages do not load, packet capture can reveal whether HTTP requests are forwarded correctly and whether responses are returned. If telnet to port eighty times out, trace the path to find where packets stop.
Misconception: Connection alone proves service health — it only shows the socket is open; application-level issues require deeper checks.
Key Takeaway

Use telnet for quick TCP port checks, then escalate to traceroute or monitor traffic depending on the outcome.

screens.title: monitor traffic — Packet capture and filtering
screens.subtitle: Capture live packets on an interface and apply filters to focus your analysis

narration.text: Monitor traffic on Junos is the operational capture tool analogous to tcpdump. It prints packet headers and, with detail options, packet contents for traffic traversing an interface. The command accepts filters to match IPs, ports, and protocols; using filters is essential because an unfiltered capture on a busy link will produce a flood of irrelevant data and can affect device responsiveness. A typical use is to monitor DNS traffic by matching port fifty-three on the outbound interface while initiating a DNS query from the router; you should see UDP packets with source or destination port fifty-three. A common pitfall is running a wide capture and trying to scan the entire output visually — instead, narrow by host, protocol, or port. When you capture the expected packets, review headers for correct source and destination addresses, ports, and protocol fields. Use monitor traffic to confirm firewall behavior or application exchanges when ping and port tests are inconclusive. monitor traffic — Packet capture and filtering means use monitor traffic to capture and inspect packets in real time; always apply filters to focus the output and protect device performance.. In practical terms, capture live packets on an interface and apply filters to focus your analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Monitor traffic
keyIdea.text: Use monitor traffic to capture and inspect packets in real time; always apply filters to focus the output and protect device performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › monitor traffic — Capture
What monitor traffic does
It observes packets on a specified interface and prints headers or detailed contents. Use it the same way you would use a capture tool on a host, but with attention to performance and filtering.
Filtering is essential
  • Filter by interface, port, host, or protocol to reduce noise.
  • Be specific: e.g., matching port fifty-three isolates DNS traffic.
  • Never run broad captures on production busy links without a clear purpose.
Example and expected output
# monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 matching "port 53"
monitor traffic on ge-0/0/0.0, link-type EN10MB, capture size 96 bytes
10:45:30.123456 Out IP 192.168.1.1.50000 > 8.8.8.8.53: UDP, length 30
10:45:30.234567 In  IP 8.8.8.8.53 > 192.168.1.1.50000: UDP, length 60
^C
Scenario card: Use a second terminal to generate traffic while the capture runs. For DNS, initiate a lookup and confirm UDP packets with port fifty-three appear in the monitor output.
Pitfall: Running monitor traffic with no filters can overwhelm consoles and make the capture useless. Apply the narrowest filter that still captures the event you need.

screens.title: A practical troubleshooting workflow
screens.subtitle: Baseline, reachability, path, service test, and packet capture — a repeatable sequence

narration.text: A reliable workflow turns tools into a method. Start by establishing a baseline: check device operational status and recent logs to rule out obvious faults. Next, verify reachability with multiple pings to your target; this tells you whether packets are making it part-way or all the way. If ping indicates failure or intermittent loss, run traceroute to identify the hop where forwarding stops. Once you know the hop, you can decide whether the problem is local, upstream, or at the destination. If the issue seems to be at a particular host or service, run a telnet to the specific TCP port to confirm whether the service is listening. If you need to inspect actual packet contents or confirm that firewall rules are allowing or dropping traffic, run monitor traffic with a focused filter against the relevant interface while generating the traffic. At each step, capture small, representative output snippets that support your diagnosis. This staged approach reduces wasted effort and gives you clear escalation steps. A practical troubleshooting workflow means follow a staged approach: baseline → ping → traceroute → service test → targeted packet capture to reach evidence-based conclusions.. In practical terms, baseline, reachability, path, service test, and packet capture — a repeatable sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Follow a staged approach: baseline → ping → traceroute → service test → targeted packet capture to reach evidence-based conclusions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Troubleshooting Workflow
Step-by-step
1. Baseline: confirm device is up, check interfaces and logs.
2. Reachability: ping the target multiple times and note loss and RTT.
3. Path: run traceroute to find the hop that fails or adds latency.
4. Service: telnet the service port or connect with SSH for management.
5. Capture: run monitor traffic with focused filters to validate packet flow.
This sequence is iterative: if monitor traffic shows packets are being dropped at a filter, adjust the filter or test different hosts until the evidence points to a configuration or device fault.
Concrete example
If ping to a web server fails, run traceroute. If the trace stops at hop two, investigate that router. If hop two is reachable but port eighty fails, telnet the server and run monitor traffic on the egress interface to confirm whether HTTP requests leave and responses return.
Key Takeaway

A measured, evidence-first sequence avoids wasted checks and leads to reproducible fixes.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: diagnosing connectivity with commands
screens.subtitle: A guided terminal demo you can follow to practice the workflow

narration.text: This hands-on sequence ties the tools together into a short lab you can repeat. First, log in to your Junos device and run status commands to confirm interfaces and routing are up. Next, test basic connectivity with ping to eight dot eight dot eight dot eight five times and record whether replies arrive and how many are lost. If ping is unsuccessful, run traceroute to the same target to find the hop where packets stop. Take note of any hop that shows asterisks. After identifying a candidate hop or server, run a telnet to the service port you want to test, for example telnet to port eighty to check HTTP. If the service is suspected of being blocked, start monitor traffic on the relevant interface with a focused filter such as matching port fifty-three for DNS or the port number you are testing. While the capture runs, generate the traffic — perform a DNS lookup or an HTTP request — then stop the capture and inspect headers for source, destination, and ports. This practical loop demonstrates how small command outputs combine into a reliable diagnosis.

keyIdea.title: Lab activity
keyIdea.text: Follow a short, repeatable demo: baseline check, ping, traceroute, telnet/SSH test, and filtered monitor traffic to collect packet-level evidence.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Hands-on Activity
Activity steps
  1. Check device and interface status to establish a baseline.
  2. Run ping 8.8.8.8 count 5 and record replies and packet loss.
  3. Run traceroute 8.8.8.8 and note the hop where responses stop.
  4. Telnet to an expected service port to test reachability of the application layer.
  5. Run monitor traffic on the egress interface with a matching filter while generating traffic, then inspect captured packets.
Starter command snippets
# ping 8.8.8.8 count 5
# traceroute 8.8.8.8
# telnet 8.8.8.8 53
# monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 matching "port 53"
Reflection prompt: if ping works but telnet fails, what does that imply about the nature of the fault? It usually indicates the path exists but the specific TCP port or service is blocked or not running.
Pro Tip

Use a second terminal for monitor traffic so you can generate traffic from the first terminal without losing the capture view.

narration.text: These core concepts are the mental shorthand you will use when troubleshooting. Ping verifies IP reachability and gives you round-trip times; it works at the network layer using ICMP. Traceroute uses the Time-To-Live mechanism to reveal intermediate hops and helps you identify the location where forwarding stops or degrades. ICMP is the supporting protocol that carries echo requests and replies, and it also carries time-exceeded messages that traceroute relies on. Keep these three concepts in mind: reachability, path, and the underlying protocol that makes these checks possible. When you see packet loss or stars in a trace, you can translate that into targeted next steps: check interfaces, inspect routing, or apply packet capture. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
ping
Tests reachability and measures round-trip time using ICMP echo requests and replies.
traceroute
Reveals the route packets take by sending probes with increasing TTL and observing time-exceeded replies.
ICMP
The protocol used for echo and time-exceeded messages that support ping and traceroute diagnostics.
Summary
Remember: ping checks reachability, traceroute finds the failing hop, and ICMP is the mechanism that carries those diagnostic messages.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Practical reminders about TTL, SSH vs telnet, and monitor traffic

narration.text: A few practical reminders will keep your troubleshooting focused. TTL, or Time-To-Live, is the field traceroute manipulates to discover hops; understanding TTL behavior lets you interpret where a trace stops. For remote checks, prefer SSH for secure management and reserve telnet for controlled port tests in labs — telnet transmits data in cleartext and is not suitable for production management. Finally, monitor traffic is powerful but potentially noisy; always apply filters such as host, port, or protocol to collect targeted evidence without overloading the device or your terminal. Together, these concepts help you choose the next command confidently: if a trace stops at a hop that does not respond, investigate that hop; if ping works but telnet fails, try a packet capture to confirm whether packets reach the expected service. Keeping these concise rules in mind reduces wasted steps and speeds diagnosis.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Think TTL for traceroute, SSH for secure access, telnet for lab port checks, and always filter monitor traffic.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
TTL
Limits packet lifetime and is the mechanism traceroute manipulates to discover intermediate hops.
SSH vs Telnet
SSH is encrypted and for management; telnet is plaintext and only for controlled lab or quick port checks.
Monitor traffic filters
Always scope captures by host, port, or protocol to avoid overwhelming output and to find relevant packets quickly.
Final takeaway
Follow the evidence: use the right tool in sequence, narrow your scope with filters, and document outputs so you can explain and repeat your diagnosis.
